title: Seasonal curve changes with warmth gave no clear later detection gain for two frogs in two US regions in 2009-2015
abstract: We tested whether a change in the seasonal calling curve with spring warmth improved later frog detection predictions. We used 12,243 distinct USGS NAAMP survey runs in 2001-2015, NOAA GHCN-CAMS temperature, wood frogs and spring peepers, and separate Northeast and Midwest samples. Models fitted in 2001-2008 were tested in 2009-2015. Route and observer intercepts, night weather, effort and a year trend controlled some observation bias. No positive log-loss gain had a 95 percent route bootstrap interval wholly above zero in any of four tests, for either a quadratic curvature term or a spline width term. Quadratic gains ranged from -0.01354 to +0.00166 nats per run; spline gains ranged from -0.00497 to +0.00099. A spline width term helped Northeast wood frog predictions in 2012, but this gain did not persist across the later period. Model form changed the Midwest wood frog event result. Quadratic wood frog peaks fell before all observed survey dates. These data do not establish biological season length. Only 24-38 percent of later runs had usable training route-observer intercepts. Sparse seasonal visits, selected returning groups, coarse climate, omitted rain and fixed-intercept bias limit inference. This study reuses records from two prior SCI studies and adds new tests of curve shape and later-period prediction. It does not test air pollution. The package supplies code, the source-attributed evidence panel, aggregate results, checks, figures and exact input hashes.
